links.outcome: Concordance of GPT-4 treatment recommendations with multidisciplinary tumor board (standard of care) decisions
links.effect: Overall concordance 73.3% (33/45), κ = 0.64; lowest with diagnostic workup (50.0% discordance) and complex cases.
links.quote: The observed agreement before literature-based prompting was 73.3% (33 cases, κ = 0.64, p < 0.0001, Fig. 1 ).

links.outcome: GPT-4 recommendations for pancreatic cancer versus guideline-based MDT decisions, including complex/serious cases
links.effect: 26.7% of cases discordant; discordance highest when MDT recommended diagnostic workup (50.0%) or resection/exploration (36.8%); additional literature prompting did not improve concordance.
links.quote: The rate of discordance was highest when the MDT recommended additional diagnostic workup (50.0%), followed by exploration/resection (36.8%), and was lowest when neoadjuvant (10.0%) or palliative systemic treatment (10.0%) was advised by the MDT (Fig. 3 B).

links.outcome: Concordance with MDT before vs after prompting GPT-4 with 41 curated abstracts
links.effect: Concordance unchanged at 73.3% (κ 0.64 to 0.61); 31 of 41 abstracts (75.4%) never cited; only 1 of 45 cases changed recommendation.
links.quote: Additional literature prompting did not result in any cases in which GPT-4’s recommendations became concordant with those of the MDT (33 cases, 73.3%, κ = 0.61, p < 0.0001, Fig. 1 ), indicating substantial agreement in both scenarios.

links.outcome: GPT-4 recommending inappropriate management in complex cases, showing unsuitability as stand-alone decision-maker
links.effect: 12 of 45 recommendations discordant with MDT; in one case GPT-4 advised resection despite CT report stating resectability could not be determined.
links.quote: While these observations remain correlative, they are consistent with the notion that LLMs, in their current form, are not capable of serving as stand-alone decision-makers and that expert judgment remains a critical factor [ 25 ].

links.outcome: GPT-4 confidence calibration when data were insufficient to determine resectability
links.effect: GPT-4 recommended resection despite CT report stating resectability could not be determined; authors attribute to poorly calibrated confidence estimates and hallucination tendency.
links.quote: Observations like these have also been made by other authors and likely reflect poorly calibrated and unreliable confidence estimates as well as the model’s tendency to produce hallucinations [ 3 , 10 , 26 , 33 , 34 ].

links.outcome: Variability of GPT-4 outputs across clinically comparable cases
links.effect: Responses were brief in some similar cases and substantially more comprehensive in others; no retry or repeated-run testing performed.
links.quote: In some instances, responses were brief and lacked contextual detail, whereas in other seemingly similar cases, they were substantially more comprehensive (Fig. 3 C/D).

links.outcome: Effect of incomplete or missing input data on GPT-4 recommendations
links.effect: Incomplete MDT referral data caused discordance in 3 of 12 non-concordant cases (25.0%); one case ignored explicit CT statement on indeterminate resectability.
links.quote: Among the 12 non-concordant cases, the presumed cause of discordance was an inadequate capture of clinical complexity by GPT-4 in three cases (25.0%), incomplete data in the MDT referral in three cases (25.0%) and a disregard of essential clinical data by GPT-4 in one case (8.3%).
